title: Why build an index with `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` on a busy table, and why should you manage every schema change through versioned migrations (Flyway/Liquibase) instead of `hibernate.ddl-auto=update` in production?
shortTitle: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY and Versioned Migrations Over hibernate.ddl-auto

s1_definition.profdef: `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` (in PostgreSQL) builds an index without taking an exclusive lock that blocks writes, so the table remains available for reads and writes during the build, at the cost of being slower and requiring two table scans. Versioned migration tools like Flyway and Liquibase apply ordered, reviewed, immutable SQL scripts to the database, giving you a controlled, auditable, reproducible schema history, whereas `hibernate.ddl-auto=update` lets Hibernate silently guess and alter the schema at startup, which is unreviewed, non-deterministic, and unsafe for production.
s1_definition.analogy: Building an index the normal way is like closing a busy National Bank of India counter to reorganize its files — customers wait. `CONCURRENTLY` is like reorganizing the files while the counter keeps serving, slower but no queue. And letting Hibernate auto-update the schema is like letting an intern rearrange the vault automatically each morning based on their best guess — sometimes right, sometimes a disaster, and nobody reviewed it. Versioned migrations are the opposite: a written, signed-off, numbered change order that is applied the same way in every branch, every time.
s1_definition.oneliner: `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` builds without blocking writes; versioned migrations give reviewed, ordered, reproducible schema changes — never let Hibernate auto-alter production.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` (in PostgreSQL) builds an index without taking an exclusive lock that blocks writes, so the table remains available for reads and writes during the build, at the cost of being slower and requiring two table scans. Versioned migration tools like Flyway and Liquibase apply ordered, reviewed, immutable SQL scripts to the database, giving you a controlled, auditable, reproducible schema history, whereas `hibernate.ddl-auto=update` lets Hibernate silently guess and alter the schema at startup, which is unreviewed, non-deterministic, and unsafe for production.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Building an index the normal way is like closing a busy National Bank of India counter to reorganize its files — customers wait. `CONCURRENTLY` is like reorganizing the files while the counter keeps serving, slower but no queue. And letting Hibernate auto-update the schema is like letting an intern rearrange the vault automatically each morning based on their best guess — sometimes right, sometimes a disaster, and nobody reviewed it. Versioned migrations are the opposite: a written, signed-off, numbered change order that is applied the same way in every branch, every time.

**One line to remember:** `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` builds without blocking writes; versioned migrations give reviewed, ordered, reproducible schema changes — never let Hibernate auto-alter production.

sections.s2_technical:
A plain `CREATE INDEX` takes a lock that blocks writes (and in some engines reads) on the table for the entire build. On a busy banking table with millions of rows, that build can take minutes, during which transactions that modify the table queue up and time out — effectively an outage. `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` solves this by building the index without that blocking lock: it scans the table once to build the index, then scans again to catch up on rows changed during the first scan, all while allowing normal reads and writes. The trade-offs are that it is slower overall, uses more resources, cannot run inside a transaction block, and can leave an invalid index behind if it fails (which you then drop and retry). But for a live production table the availability benefit is decisive. The same philosophy applies to other DDL: prefer the non-blocking or short-lock variant (add nullable columns, validate constraints in two phases, drop concurrently where supported) so you never freeze a live table.

The second half is about how schema changes are managed. `hibernate.ddl-auto` has modes like `none`, `validate`, `update`, and `create-drop`. The `update` mode makes Hibernate compare its entity mappings to the live schema at startup and automatically issue ALTERs to reconcile them. This is convenient in local development but dangerous in production for several reasons. It is non-deterministic — the generated DDL depends on Hibernate's version and dialect and may differ between environments, so what runs in staging may not match production. It is unreviewed — nobody sees or approves the SQL before it hits the database, so a seemingly innocent entity change can trigger a destructive or table-rewriting ALTER. It never drops or renames safely — `update` only adds, so removed fields leave orphaned columns and renames become add-plus-orphan. It gives no rollback and no history — there is no versioned record of what changed when. And it can take long locks unpredictably at startup, delaying or breaking a deployment.

Versioned migration tools fix all of this. With Flyway or Liquibase you write each schema change as a numbered, immutable script (`V2__add_index.sql`), check it into version control, review it in a pull request, and the tool applies pending scripts in order exactly once, recording each in a schema-history table. This gives you a deterministic, reproducible schema across every environment, a reviewable change (so you catch a dangerous ALTER before it runs), an auditable history of who changed what and when, and a forward-fix or rollback path. In production you set `hibernate.ddl-auto=validate` (or `none`), which makes Hibernate only verify that the live schema matches the entities and refuse to start if not, while all actual changes go through migrations. This combination — migrations own the schema, Hibernate only validates — is the industry standard for safe database evolution.

The senior synthesis: you combine both ideas. Schema changes are expressed as reviewed, versioned migrations, and within those migrations you use non-blocking DDL like `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` (noting Flyway must run such statements outside a transaction) so that the ordered, auditable change is also a zero-downtime change on a busy table.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem — National Bank of India had two incidents. First, a developer ran a plain `CREATE INDEX` on the 300-million-row `transactions` table during peak hours; it held a write lock for eight minutes and payment transactions timed out — a partial outage. Second, a service ran with `hibernate.ddl-auto=update` in production, and a refactor that renamed a field caused Hibernate to add a new column and silently orphan the old one, leaving data stranded and the schema inconsistent with staging. The platform team mandated two rules: all indexes on busy tables are created with `CONCURRENTLY`, and all schema changes go through Flyway with `ddl-auto=validate`.

Our mini-project demonstrates the concepts: a `MigrationPlan` that represents ordered Flyway-style versioned scripts, a check that a concurrent index build does not block simulated concurrent writes, and a `Demo` contrasting blocking versus concurrent index behavior and validate-versus-update config.

The code will contain: a `Migration` record-like class, a `MigrationRunner` that applies ordered migrations and records history, an `IndexBuildSim` showing blocking versus concurrent effect on concurrent writers, and a `Demo`.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run
java -cp target/migration-governance-1.0.0.jar com.bank.gov.GovApplication

# Expected:
# Migrations applied in order V2, V6; V6 runs outside a transaction (concurrent DDL)
# Writes during PLAIN build: low (writers blocked by the index lock)
# Writes during CONCURRENT build: high (writers proceed)
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: two versioned migrations (V2 add nullable column, V6 add index concurrently) and a simulation of ten concurrent writers during an index build.

Step 1: The migration runner sorts the migrations by version and applies each exactly once, recording it in a simulated schema-history set. V2 runs inside a transaction; V6, being a concurrent index build, is flagged to run outside a transaction, mirroring how Flyway must handle `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`. This is the ordered, auditable, apply-once behavior that replaces Hibernate guessing.

Step 2: Re-running would skip already-applied versions, which is the idempotent, deterministic property that makes migrations safe across environments — unlike `ddl-auto=update`, which re-derives DDL each startup.

Step 3: The index-build simulation first runs a plain build, which holds a write lock. The ten writers block until the build finishes, so very few writes complete during the build window — this models the eight-minute payment outage the bank suffered.

Step 4: The simulation then runs a concurrent build, which does not hold the blocking lock. The writers proceed throughout, so most or all writes complete during the build — this models `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` keeping the table available.

Step 5: The demo prints both the ordered migration application and the stark difference in writes completed, showing why busy-table indexes use `CONCURRENTLY` and why schema changes go through reviewed migrations.

```
Oct 25, 2026 17:04:00 INFO: Running V2 in a transaction
Oct 25, 2026 17:04:00 INFO:   -> ALTER TABLE accounts ADD COLUMN x NUMERIC NULL
Oct 25, 2026 17:04:00 INFO: Running V6 OUTSIDE a transaction (concurrent DDL)
Oct 25, 2026 17:04:00 INFO:   -> CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_txn_account ON transactions(account_id)
Oct 25, 2026 17:04:00 INFO: Applied versions: [2, 6]
Writes during PLAIN build: 2 (blocked)
Writes during CONCURRENT build: 10 (not blocked)
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Schema change needed
    │
    ▼  write Flyway script → PR review → merge (ordered, immutable)
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ V2 ALTER ADD COLUMN NULL   (in txn)            │
  │ V6 CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY (outside txn)     │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘
    │  MigrationRunner applies in order, once, records history
    ▼
  ┌───────────── index build on busy transactions table ─────────────┐
  │ PLAIN:        write lock held → writers BLOCK → outage            │
  │ CONCURRENTLY: no blocking lock → writers PROCEED → available      │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
    │  prod config: hibernate.ddl-auto = validate (migrations own schema)
    ▼  deterministic, reviewed, auditable, reproducible
```
sections.s5c_hld:
```
  ═══ HLD — Schema Change Governance ═══

  ┌──────────┐ PR  ┌─────────────┐ merge ┌──────────────────────┐
  │ Developer│────→│ Code Review │──────→│ CI/CD Pipeline        │
  │ (Flyway  │     │ (approve DDL)│       │ runs Flyway migrate   │
  │  script) │     └─────────────┘       └──────────┬───────────┘
  └──────────┘                                      │ ordered, once
                                                    ▼
                                 ┌──────────────────────────────┐
                                 │ PostgreSQL                     │
                                 │ flyway_schema_history (audit) │
                                 │ CONCURRENTLY for busy indexes  │
                                 └──────────────────────────────┘
  App: hibernate.ddl-auto=validate → fails fast if schema ≠ entities
```

Every DDL is reviewed, versioned, and applied by CI through Flyway; the app only validates the schema, and busy-table indexes are built concurrently.
sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Migrations + Non-Blocking DDL ═══

  ┌─ Rules ──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Busy-table index → CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY (no wlock)   │
  │   (Flyway: run outside transaction)                       │
  │ Schema changes → versioned Flyway/Liquibase scripts       │
  │ Prod Hibernate → ddl-auto=validate (never update)         │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ──
  ┌──────────────────────────┐   ┌──────────────┐
  │ MigrationRunner          │──▶│ Migration    │
  │ + apply(list)            │   │ version,sql, │
  │ - applied: history       │   │ concurrent   │
  └──────────────────────────┘   └──────────────┘
  ┌──────────────────────────┐
  │ IndexBuildSim            │  shows blocking vs concurrent
  │ + simulate(concurrent)   │
  └──────────────────────────┘

  ── Call Chain ──
  1. apply([V2,V6]) → sort → run each once → record history
  2. V6 runs outside txn (CONCURRENTLY)
  3. simulate(false) → writers blocked
  4. simulate(true)  → writers proceed
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
I build an index on a busy table with `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` because a plain `CREATE INDEX` takes a lock that blocks writes for the whole build, and on a table with hundreds of millions of rows that build can last minutes, during which live transactions queue up and time out — effectively an outage. The concurrent build scans the table without that blocking lock, letting reads and writes continue; the trade-offs are that it is slower, uses more resources, cannot run inside a transaction, and can leave an invalid index if it fails, which I drop and retry, but on a live production table the availability is worth it. The same philosophy applies to all DDL — prefer the non-blocking or short-lock variant so I never freeze a live table.

For managing schema changes I use versioned migrations with Flyway or Liquibase rather than `hibernate.ddl-auto=update` in production, and I set `ddl-auto=validate` so Hibernate only checks that the live schema matches the entities and refuses to start if not, while all real changes go through migrations. The reason is that `update` is non-deterministic across Hibernate versions and dialects, unreviewed so a small entity change can trigger a destructive or table-rewriting ALTER nobody approved, only additive so removed fields orphan columns and renames become add-plus-orphan, and it keeps no history and offers no rollback. Versioned migrations are ordered, immutable, reviewed in a pull request, applied exactly once, and recorded in a schema-history table, giving a reproducible schema across every environment. In our National Bank of India systems a plain index build on the 300-million-row transactions table once locked writes for eight minutes and timed out payments, and a service running `ddl-auto=update` once orphaned a column during a rename and drifted from staging — after both incidents we mandated `CONCURRENTLY` for busy-table indexes and Flyway with `ddl-auto=validate`. The senior synthesis I give is that I combine the two: changes are reviewed versioned migrations, and inside them I use non-blocking DDL like `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`, run outside a transaction, so the change is both auditable and zero-downtime. The line I remember is: build busy indexes concurrently to avoid blocking writes, and own the schema with reviewed versioned migrations while Hibernate only validates.
